finding.claim: DELETE /files/<fid> has no effective authorization check. require_allowed (is_allowed) returns a bool that is discarded, so any caller can delete any file record.
finding.source: HTTP DELETE request to /files/<fid>; the caller needs no grant on the file (views.py:15-16)

trace.note: load_user sets g.user from the X-Session-User-Verified header
require_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') calls is_allowed, which returns a bool; the result is not checked, so nothing aborts
is_allowed returns a bool and does not raise
ensure_allowed is the enforcing variant that aborts with 403; the delete route does not use it

finding.guards_checked: acl.is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) returns False for unauthorized users but nothing acts on it. The rename route uses ensure_allowed (views.py:26) correctly. The import alias at views.py:4 hides that the delete check is a predicate. Caveat: no code in this repo populates STORE, so routes raise KeyError at views.py:17 until STORE is populated elsewhere.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. acl.is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) returns a bool, and the delete route calls it as a bare statement at views.py:18 with the result discarded, so nothing aborts before `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19. The enforcing variant ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, abort(403)) is imported under that name at views.py:3 but is not used by delete_file. The rename route at views.py:26 does use ensure_allowed.
verdict.reason: The delete route at views.py:18 discards the bool from require_allowed (is_allowed, acl.py:4-5), so the unconditional `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19 runs for any caller, including an anonymous one, and nothing in the repo blocks it. The caveat stands: nothing in this repo populates STORE, so the route raises KeyError at views.py:17 unless something elsewhere fills it, and identity comes from a client-settable header (views.py:12), which only matters once a check exists.

finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from a client-supplied header with no verification, so any client can impersonate any user and inherit that user's grants. Severity depends on whether the edge proxy overwrites this header.
finding.source: Request header X-Session-User-Verified, fully attacker-controlled unless an upstream component sets it (views.py:12)
finding.sink: Every ACL decision that uses g.user: delete authorization (views.py:18) and rename authorization (views.py:26), via grants lookup in acl.py:5

trace.note: before_request load_user runs on every request
g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') copies the raw header value with no signature, session, or trust check
action in resource.get('grants', {}).get(user, []) uses the spoofed user as the grants key
ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'write') on rename trusts the spoofed identity

finding.guards_checked: No validation, stripping, or session lookup of the header exists in this repo. The header name suggests an upstream verifier, but none is present. If the edge always overwrites or strips this header on external traffic, the risk is much smaller; this cannot be confirmed from the repo.

verdict.guard_found: Rename is gated by ensure_allowed (views.py:26, acl.py:8-10), which aborts with 403 on failure, but it checks the same client-supplied header identity, so it does not block spoofing. Delete has no effective guard: require_allowed (is_allowed, acl.py:4-5) returns a bool that views.py:18 discards, so the delete check never runs.
verdict.reason: The header is read unverified at views.py:12 and used as the grants key at acl.py:5, so rename (views.py:26) can be spoofed if the edge does not overwrite X-Session-User-Verified, but that edge behavior is not in the repo. The trace misdescribes views.py:18: the is_allowed result is discarded, so delete is unchecked for any caller regardless of the header, which is a separate and more serious defect the candidate does not state.
